title: Trump Mass-Revokes Security Clearances of Political Opponents and Critics
description_short: Trump Mass-Revokes Security Clearances of Political Opponents and Critics
description_medium: Over February and March 2025, the Trump administration revoked security clearances from former officials and critics. Joe Biden’s revocation was dated February 7, followed by Antony Blinken and Jake Sullivan on February 8–9; a March 22 memo listed more figures. Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard separately removed dozens of intelligence officials.
description_long: In early 2025, the Trump administration revoked security clearances from former officials and other critics. Joe Biden’s clearance was revoked on February 7, followed by those of Antony Blinken and Jake Sullivan on February 8 and 9. A separate March 22 memo named Kamala Harris, Hillary Clinton, members of Biden’s family, Liz Cheney, Alexander Vindman, Fiona Hill, Adam Kinzinger, attorney Mark Zaid, and New York officials Letitia James and Alvin Bragg. Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard separately removed dozens of current and former intelligence officials. The actions therefore involved distinct groups and dates, rather than one list acted on at the same time. Security clearances grant access to classified information, and these decisions affected former officials, political figures, prosecutors, and critics. The available facts do not describe individual security findings or the review process behind the revocations. They establish a series of clearance actions but leave the stated justification and the relationship among the separate decisions unresolved.

title: Jack Smith Final Report: Evidence Was Sufficient to Convict Trump
description_short: Jack Smith Final Report: Evidence Was Sufficient to Convict Trump
description_medium: On January 14, 2025, the Justice Department released the election subversion investigation’s final report by Special Counsel Jack Smith. Smith said admissible evidence could support a conviction at trial and attributed the absence of prosecution to the department’s policy against prosecuting a sitting president. His assessment was not a jury verdict; the case did not go to trial.
description_long: On January 14, 2025, six days before Trump’s inauguration, the Justice Department released Volume I of Special Counsel Jack Smith’s final report into efforts to overturn the 2020 election. Smith wrote that admissible evidence was sufficient to obtain and sustain a conviction at trial. That was the prosecutor’s assessment of what the evidence could support, not a verdict or conviction: the case did not proceed to trial. The report described actions Smith called criminal efforts to retain power, including false claims of election fraud and pressure on Vice President Mike Pence. It also recounted Trump’s private reaction after Joe Biden appeared on television and his frustration with Pence. Smith said the Justice Department’s longstanding policy against prosecuting a sitting president prevented prosecution after Trump returned to office. Trump rejected the report, calling Smith a “lamebrain prosecutor.” The document preserved the special counsel’s account of the evidence and the reason he gave for the case ending without trial, while leaving no jury adjudication of the allegations.

description_short: President Trump threatened using the Insurrection Act on Truth Social in response to ongoing protest in Minneapolis after the killing of Renee Good by ICE
description_medium: On January 15, 2026, President Donald Trump threatened on Truth Social to use the Insurrection Act in response to protests in Minneapolis after Renee Good was killed by an ICE officer. The supplied account documents a threat, not an invocation of the Act or a deployment of federal forces. The protest events and any later government action are not described.
description_long: On January 15, 2026, President Donald Trump posted on Truth Social that he might use the Insurrection Act in response to protests in Minneapolis following the killing of Renee Good by an ICE officer. The post came amid ongoing local protests. It describes a threat, not a documented invocation: no order, deployment of federal forces, or other implementation is identified in the supplied facts. That distinction matters because a public warning can signal possible federal intervention without establishing what the government actually did. Use of the Act would also raise questions about federal and local authority over public order. The account gives no details about the protests’ size or events, state or local officials’ response, the administration’s stated legal justification, or subsequent steps. The reported episode is a presidential threat during protests after Good’s killing; the supplied facts do not establish that it led to an operational consequence.

title: Leo Garcia Venegas: US Citizen Detained Three Times in ICE Racial Profiling Stops
description_short: Leo Garcia Venegas: US Citizen Detained Three Times in ICE Racial Profiling Stops
description_medium: Leo Garcia Venegas, an Alabama construction worker and U.S. citizen, was detained by immigration agents while filming his brother’s arrest. He later testified before Congress and filed a federal lawsuit. ProPublica reported that ICE official Todd Lyons acknowledged citizen detentions could serve as a deterrent. Venegas’ case focuses attention on citizens’ treatment during immigration enforcement and allegations that appearance, work and language shaped stops.
description_long: Leo Garcia Venegas, a U.S. citizen and Alabama construction worker, was detained by immigration agents three separate times through May 2026. The first incident in mid-2025 involved agents tackling him while he filmed his brother's arrest at a construction site, ignoring his citizenship claims. A few weeks later, an officer at a home he was building refused to trust his Alabama REAL ID — which only citizens and legal residents can obtain. Videos went viral; Garcia Venegas testified before Congress and filed a federal lawsuit. Despite the pending lawsuit, he was detained a third time in May 2026. The same week, masked agents in the Bronx tackled an American teenager who, once identified as a citizen, was left bloody and bruised in an unfamiliar neighborhood. ProPublica reported that in response to its coverage, ICE official Todd Lyons acknowledged citizen detentions serve as a deterrent. His attorney argued the stops constitute racial profiling stops based on the Supreme Court's fall 2024 ruling permitting stops partly based on apparent ethnicity, job in construction, and speaking Spanish. Despite three documented detentions, ICE denied his damage claim in April 2026 with no explanation, then detained him again two weeks later.

title: Jermaine Thomas, Born on US Army Base in Germany, Deported to Jamaica He'd Never Visited
description_short: Jermaine Thomas, Born on US Army Base in Germany, Deported to Jamaica He'd Never Visited
description_medium: A July 2025 fact-check published by Yahoo, citing ICE and DHS, says Jermaine Thomas was deported to Jamaica on May 28, 2025, after courts rejected his U.S. citizenship claim. It reports that an immigration judge had issued a final removal order in 2013. Thomas was born in Germany to a U.S.-citizen father serving in the Army. His case centers on birth abroad to a U.S. servicemember and the legal process that led to his removal.
description_long: In late May 2025, Jermaine Thomas, 39, was shackled at the wrists and ankles and placed on a flight to Kingston, Jamaica — a country he had never been to in his life. Thomas was born in 1986 at a US military hospital in Germany, where his father — a US citizen — was deployed as an Army soldier. His case had reached the US Supreme Court ten years earlier in a dispute over whether children born to US citizen servicemembers on overseas deployments should automatically receive citizenship. The court ruled against him. Thomas had no citizenship anywhere: not the United States (despite his father's decades of military service), not Germany (where he was born), not Jamaica (his father's ancestral homeland), and not Kenya (his mother's birthplace). When reached by CNN, Thomas described himself as legally stateless, calling from a homeless shelter in Kingston. He had no passport, no support network, and no connection to the country. DHS issued a statement calling him a violent, criminal illegal alien from Jamaica and describing Jamaica as his home country — a characterization the Austin Chronicle challenged in direct correspondence with the department, asking in what sense Jamaica was his home country. DHS did not respond. Thomas's case illustrates how the Trump administration's deportation framework was being applied even to people abandoned by the citizenship system because of technical legal gaps — leaving a man stateless on the basis of his father's military service.
